newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk farm sector faces doubts with new government.
newsitem.headline: Turk farm sector faces doubts with new government.

text.p: Turkish agricultural producers and traders said on Thursday they faced uncertainty over the implementation of pledges made by the Islamist-led government, which has stepped down under secularist pressure.
"The (Islamist-led) government gave good prices to please farmers and to draw their votes," a trader from a Western trading house told Reuters.

"But it has not published the required decrees for grain and sugar beet purchases. Do we really know if the new government will uphold the same prices announced by the predecessor?" asked the trader, who declined to be named.

On Wednesday night, Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan submitted his coalition government's resignation to President Suleyman Demirel, who asked him to carry on as caretaker until a new government is formed.

Demirel is meeting opposition party leaders on Thursday and is to nominate one of them to form a government that is likely to take the country to early general elections either later this year or early in 1998.
"The new government will have to find answers to questions like how the finances will be provided, to what degree it can keep the promise of grain purchases," said the Western trader.

Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller, head of the conservative wing of the fallen coalition, announced this week a 1997/98 sugar beet base price at 11,000 per kg, up 150 percent from a year earlier and close to beet growers' demand of 11,500 lira.
Last month Erbakan's government announced a grain base price rise for 1997/98 of 83.3 percent on average, compared with an annual inflation rate of about 75 percent in May.
Kamil Ozdemir, head of sugar beet purchasing cooperatives union Pankobirlik, said the government gave "favourable" beet prices this year which were welcomed by growers.
"But we do not want to doubt that the new goverment may modify the announced prices," he told Reuters.
But Ali Guvenir, deputy general manager of Ozkasikci flour mills and a wheat trader, said: "These are populist policies, investments for elections."

Erbakan, whose policies and practices were strongly criticised by the powerful army for undermining the secularist establishment, said in May he wanted early general elections in October to resolve the political upheaval.

Officials said the state grain board (TMO) would buy about 3.7 million tonnes of grain, 2.2 million tonnes of that being wheat and one million tonnes barley, from farmers in 1997/98 after anticipation of good grain output.

Turkey's foreign trade undersecretariat prepared a decree earlier this month to raise a wheat import tax from the current 15 percent to protect farmers and curb imports. The decree has not come before the caretaker government yet.
The TMO also has plans to raise the corn import tax in the autumn, when the first corn crop comes on the market.
The Western trader said any new government would have to wield the import tax to regulate incoming grain and to divert flour mills to using local wheat.
"By raising import taxes the government may limit imports and help realise its own grain purchasing plans," he said.

With declared grain base prices, the TMO, which has about $140 million in its coffers, needs about $800 million to finance all of the planned purchases. A TMO team is bargaining in London to borrow about $400 to $500 million in syndication loans.

The agriculture ministry is also studying a plan to enable the government to fix grain import taxes at par to world prices through an intervention commission, made up of ministry and grain officials, producers and traders.

Officials said the need to increase the wheat import tax had arisen after Turkey's initial estimates that it would produce around 18 million tonnes of wheat in 1997/98, up from 16.5 million tonnes a year ago.
Unofficial estimates by millers show Turkey's 1996/97 wheat imports were about two million tonnes and a similar figure could be expected in 1997/98.
Ilker Tanik, head of the Millers' Association, said Turkey would have up to 17 million tonnes of wheat production in 1997/98 and it had a carry-over stock of two million tonnes from 1996/97.

Ozdemir reiterated earlier estimates that Turkey would produce about 2.05 million tonnes of sugar in 1997/98, up from 1.85 million tonnes a year earlier and the base prices announced by the Erbakan government "will help fulfil the target."
